paragraphs.text: For much of modern history, smell has been treated as the poor relation of the human senses. Philosophers ranked it below sight and hearing, regarding it as crude and animal-like, and nineteenth-century anatomists seemed to supply evidence for that prejudice. Comparing brains, they noticed that the olfactory bulb, the structure that first receives signals from the nose, occupies a far smaller share of the human brain than it does in dogs or rodents. From this they concluded that humans had traded a keen nose for a larger thinking cortex. The idea proved remarkably durable, passing from textbooks into popular belief, and only in recent decades has it been seriously challenged.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: To understand why, it helps to know how smelling actually works. When we breathe in, molecules released by objects around us travel to a small patch of tissue high in the nasal cavity, roughly the size of a postage stamp. There, millions of sensory nerve cells carry receptors on hair-like projections bathed in mucus. Humans possess around 400 different types of working receptor, and each type responds to a range of molecules rather than to a single one. A given odour therefore activates a particular combination of receptors, rather like a chord played on a piano, and the brain learns to recognise the pattern. Because the number of possible combinations is enormous, a modest set of receptors can distinguish a vast number of smells. Unusually for nerve cells, these sensory cells are not permanent: they are replaced regularly throughout life, roughly every one to two months.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The route these signals take inside the brain is equally distinctive. Information from the eyes, ears and skin passes through a relay station called the thalamus before reaching the brain's outer layers. Smell signals, by contrast, travel from the olfactory bulb straight to regions involved in emotion, such as the amygdala, and to areas closely tied to memory. This short path may explain why a particular scent — a grandparent's kitchen, the polish on a school corridor — can bring back a vivid scene from childhood before we have even identified what we are smelling. In one study by the psychologist Folasade Wren, volunteers given smells as memory cues recalled events that were, on average, older and more emotionally charged than those prompted by written words or photographs. However, they rated these smell-cued memories as less clear in their details.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: If the machinery is so sophisticated, why did the belief in a weak human nose persist for so long? Part of the answer lies in that original anatomical comparison. The neuroscientist Oskar Lindwall argues that judging the bulb against total brain size was misleading. When his team counted nerve cells instead of comparing proportions, they found that the human olfactory bulb contains roughly as many neurons as those of several mammals famed for their sense of smell. 'A small room in a large house is still a room,' Lindwall remarks. 'The human bulb looks modest only because everything around it grew.'
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Behavioural evidence points in the same direction. Malika Duchesne, who studies sensory perception, tested how little of certain substances needed to be present in the air before people could notice them. For a handful of compounds, including one that gives bananas their scent, her volunteers responded at concentrations as low as those previously recorded for dogs and mice. Duchesne is careful not to overstate the result: dogs remain far better at most tasks, particularly at following a scent trail across the ground. Her point is rather that human ability varies greatly from one substance to another, so sweeping claims that humans smell badly conceal a more complicated picture.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A further reason for the underestimation is linguistic. Most European languages have few words reserved for smells; speakers tend to describe an odour by naming its source, as in 'it smells like smoke', rather than with abstract terms comparable to 'red' or 'loud'. The linguist Hyun-woo Baek suggests that this poverty of vocabulary has been mistaken for a poverty of perception. In his experiments, adults who spent several weeks learning invented names for twenty unfamiliar odours became noticeably better at telling similar smells apart, while a control group who simply sniffed the same samples without labels improved only slightly. For Baek, the trouble many people have in identifying smells reflects a lack of practice and vocabulary rather than any weakness in the nose itself.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Interest in smell has grown sharply in recent years, partly because so many people temporarily lost the sense during the COVID-19 pandemic. Their experiences revealed how much it contributes to everyday life. Without it, food becomes dull, since much of what we call taste is in fact smell, as odours rise to the nose from the back of the mouth while we chew. Many sufferers also reported feeling isolated or low. Smell training, which involves sniffing a set of strong odours twice a day over several months, is now seen as a promising aid to recovery, although its effectiveness is still being investigated. Far from being a leftover from our animal past, the human nose appears to be a capable and underused instrument.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
The Underrated Nose

A. For much of modern history, smell has been treated as the poor relation of the human senses. Philosophers ranked it below sight and hearing, regarding it as crude and animal-like, and nineteenth-century anatomists seemed to supply evidence for that prejudice. Comparing brains, they noticed that the olfactory bulb, the structure that first receives signals from the nose, occupies a far smaller share of the human brain than it does in dogs or rodents. From this they concluded that humans had traded a keen nose for a larger thinking cortex. The idea proved remarkably durable, passing from textbooks into popular belief, and only in recent decades has it been seriously challenged.

B. To understand why, it helps to know how smelling actually works. When we breathe in, molecules released by objects around us travel to a small patch of tissue high in the nasal cavity, roughly the size of a postage stamp. There, millions of sensory nerve cells carry receptors on hair-like projections bathed in mucus. Humans possess around 400 different types of working receptor, and each type responds to a range of molecules rather than to a single one. A given odour therefore activates a particular combination of receptors, rather like a chord played on a piano, and the brain learns to recognise the pattern. Because the number of possible combinations is enormous, a modest set of receptors can distinguish a vast number of smells. Unusually for nerve cells, these sensory cells are not permanent: they are replaced regularly throughout life, roughly every one to two months.

C. The route these signals take inside the brain is equally distinctive. Information from the eyes, ears and skin passes through a relay station called the thalamus before reaching the brain's outer layers. Smell signals, by contrast, travel from the olfactory bulb straight to regions involved in emotion, such as the amygdala, and to areas closely tied to memory. This short path may explain why a particular scent — a grandparent's kitchen, the polish on a school corridor — can bring back a vivid scene from childhood before we have even identified what we are smelling. In one study by the psychologist Folasade Wren, volunteers given smells as memory cues recalled events that were, on average, older and more emotionally charged than those prompted by written words or photographs. However, they rated these smell-cued memories as less clear in their details.

D. If the machinery is so sophisticated, why did the belief in a weak human nose persist for so long? Part of the answer lies in that original anatomical comparison. The neuroscientist Oskar Lindwall argues that judging the bulb against total brain size was misleading. When his team counted nerve cells instead of comparing proportions, they found that the human olfactory bulb contains roughly as many neurons as those of several mammals famed for their sense of smell. 'A small room in a large house is still a room,' Lindwall remarks. 'The human bulb looks modest only because everything around it grew.'

E. Behavioural evidence points in the same direction. Malika Duchesne, who studies sensory perception, tested how little of certain substances needed to be present in the air before people could notice them. For a handful of compounds, including one that gives bananas their scent, her volunteers responded at concentrations as low as those previously recorded for dogs and mice. Duchesne is careful not to overstate the result: dogs remain far better at most tasks, particularly at following a scent trail across the ground. Her point is rather that human ability varies greatly from one substance to another, so sweeping claims that humans smell badly conceal a more complicated picture.

F. A further reason for the underestimation is linguistic. Most European languages have few words reserved for smells; speakers tend to describe an odour by naming its source, as in 'it smells like smoke', rather than with abstract terms comparable to 'red' or 'loud'. The linguist Hyun-woo Baek suggests that this poverty of vocabulary has been mistaken for a poverty of perception. In his experiments, adults who spent several weeks learning invented names for twenty unfamiliar odours became noticeably better at telling similar smells apart, while a control group who simply sniffed the same samples without labels improved only slightly. For Baek, the trouble many people have in identifying smells reflects a lack of practice and vocabulary rather than any weakness in the nose itself.

G. Interest in smell has grown sharply in recent years, partly because so many people temporarily lost the sense during the COVID-19 pandemic. Their experiences revealed how much it contributes to everyday life. Without it, food becomes dull, since much of what we call taste is in fact smell, as odours rise to the nose from the back of the mouth while we chew. Many sufferers also reported feeling isolated or low. Smell training, which involves sniffing a set of strong odours twice a day over several months, is now seen as a promising aid to recovery, although its effectiveness is still being investigated. Far from being a leftover from our animal past, the human nose appears to be a capable and underused instrument.
